details:
Project identity and summary

Project Name: Nova Knights

Selected Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Nova Knights Adventure is a free browser game that trains children aged 7 to 12 to think like Mars mission crew. The child runs a Mars base. Each Mars day an alarm goes off in one room: a solar storm, a hot battery, a clogged water recycler. The child has a few seconds to pick one of two choices, plays a short skill mini game to do it, then gives each of the four astronauts a job before night falls.

It addresses the challenge by teaching real mission trade-offs through play instead of reading. Every choice shows what it costs, what it gives and what may happen later, and no choice is free. Oxygen, water, food, power and the radiation shield all run down, so the child must balance mission against keeping the crew safe.

The problems come from real NASA data. The storms are real records from NASA's DONKI space-weather database, and each of the 24 problems carries a NASA fact with a source the player can open.

It matters because most space content for children is either posters of facts or simulators that are too hard. This game lets a 9-year-old feel why mission decisions are difficult. It needs no download, login or personal data, and it works on a cheap phone or a classroom projector.

What it does?

The player commands a four-person Mars outpost. There are two modes:

Casual: 7 Mars days. Send 20 science stars to Earth and keep the crew's radiation badge out of the red.

Survival: no last day. Alarms get faster each day, down to 4 seconds, and the run ends when food, water or oxygen runs out or radiation gets too high. Scores go on a high-score board.

Each day follows the same loop:

1) Alarm: A problem appears in one room of the base, with a countdown.

2) Choose a tool: Two tools are offered. Each lists its costs and what it gives, then what may happen later.

3) Mini game: A short skill game applies the tool. There are 26 different ones, such as cranking, tracing, wiring and sorting.
4) Crew jobs: Each astronaut gets one job: lab science, refill oxygen, dig ice for water, garden, repair or rest.

5) Night: Supplies are used up; results arrive and the base changes visibly.

o   A guide character, Nova, teaches the first day with a spoken tutorial. Nothing is scary: if the mission fails, "Mission Control brings the crew home safely". Every ending shows what happened, which choice caused it and a true NASA story about a similar situation.

o   Rewards keep children coming back: 19 badges that pay stars during play, five ranks and a shop with 32 base decorations. A Training room lets them practice each mini-game and see "why this tool matters" cards with real NASA photographs.

 

How does it work?

A rules engine holds all the game logic. It is deterministic: the same seed always gives the same game, so every rule can be tested. All game content (60 events, of which 24 are in the kid game) is generated from one written specification, where each science fact carries a numbered source.

An automatic content check fails the build if any action card has no cost. This is how "no free lunch" is enforced.

A simulator plays thousands of games with five strategies to check balance. In 1,000 simulated games a crew that only does science never win, and balanced play wins about three games in four.

Benefits

o   Children learn systems thinking: every gain has a cost, and upkeep matters as much as discovery.

o   They meet real space science in context: radiation, life support, power budgets and communication delay.

o   Teachers can use it in one lesson. A teacher guide is included, and a game takes about 10 minutes.

o   It is safe and accessible: no accounts, tracking or adverts. It has large tap targets, readable text and keyboard control, and it never relies on color alone.

What we hope to achieve

We want children to finish a game able to explain one real trade-off a Mars crew faces, and curious enough to open the NASA source behind it. Next steps are playtests with children in the target age range, an Arabic version, and a "today's Sun" mode that reads live DONKI data.

Tools and technology

Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS, with Python for one build script.

Frameworks and build: Preact, Vite, Vitest (145 automated tests).

Graphics and sound: all art is SVG drawn in code. Sound effects and ambience are synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API.

Voice: Nova's tutorial voice is computer speech from Piper, an open-source text-to-speech engine, using a voice trained on public-domain recordings.

Data: NASA DONKI API, NASA OSDR, NASA mission pages and NASA image library.

Assets: Twemoji icons (CC-BY 4.0), Atkinson Hyperlegible font (OFL).

Hosting: Vercel. Play at https://nova-knights-hazel.vercel.app/

AI use: the code and game text were written with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code), directed and reviewed by the team. No AI-generated images, video or music are in the game.

How is your project creative?

The creativity of Nova Knights Adventure lies not just in being an educational game, but in how it integrates real NASA scientific data into an engaging, simplified experience tailored for children (ages 7 to 12), through the following innovations:

  • Play-Based Real-World Trade-offs (No "Free Lunch" Rule): Unlike traditional games that give players free rewards, every choice in the game has an immediate or future cost and consequence (such as balancing oxygen, water, and power), teaching children strategic thinking and real resource management.
  • Direct Integration of Real NASA Science (DONKI & Real Data): Solar storms and technical glitches are not random; they are pulled from real NASA logs (such as the May 2024 solar storms and solar-weather data from the DONKI database). With every problem a child faces, an authentic scientific fact and a verifiable source are available to open.
  • Interactive Storytelling with a Friendly Guide (Nova): A welcoming digital guide named Nova uses a calm, computer-generated voice (powered by Piper text-to-speech) to make children feel safe. Even if a mission fails, they are met with a reassuring message from "Mission Control bringing the crew home safely."
  • Zero-Friction, Lightweight Web Architecture: The game runs smoothly directly in any browser with no login, downloads, or user tracking required, making it instantly accessible on cheap smartphones or classroom projectors.

What factors did your team consider?

During the design and development of the project, the team carefully factored in several critical pedagogical, technical, and accessibility standards:

  • Pedagogical Alignment & Target Age Group: The interface was designed specifically for children (7-12 years old) using highly readable typography (Atkinson Hyperlegible), large tap targets, and non-frightening mechanics. Each game takes about 10 minutes, making it ideal for a single classroom lesson.
  • Scientific Accuracy & Complete Transparency: While game mechanics are streamlined for pacing (e.g., speeding up processes by 15x), the team maintained strict honesty. A dedicated data screen clearly distinguishes between fun "game rules" and authentic "NASA facts."
  • Rigorous Balance Simulation & Automated Testing: To ensure the game is neither impossible nor trivial, the team built a simulator that ran over 1,000 automated test games across five strategies, proving that balanced play wins roughly three out of four games. They also wrote 145 automated code tests to ensure total system reliability.
  • Accessibility & Lightweight Tech Stack: Built using clean, modern web technologies (TypeScript, Preact, Vite), SVG graphics coded directly, and local browser audio synthesis (Web Audio API), the game ensures full keyboard and touch accessibility without relying on color alone to convey critical information.
dataRefs: Provided an archived snapshot of May 2024 (the strongest solar storm period in two decades). The game uses three real records with their actual dates: the X3.9 solar flare (10 May 2024), the WSA-ENLIL model run predicting a cloud arrival at Mars (13 May 2024), and the particle event of 13 May 2024. These power the solar storm events in both game modes (labelled as archived replays with links to the records).

Provided the baseline Mars surface radiation dose (~0.64 mSv/day) and data on the 20 May 2024 surge (8,100 micrograys at Gale Crater). These figures directly shape the crew’s radiation badge status and the radiation-storm mechanics.
The 600 mSv career limit and 250 mSv single-storm limit set the scale for the crew's radiation badges, while the ECLSS data defines daily food, water, and oxygen consumption parameters per astronaut.
Provided the biological study showing mice losing muscle and bone in 33 days on the ISS, which informs the crew exercise event and maintenance requirements.
projectRefs: Serves as an auxiliary reference for solar flare observation and coronal mass ejection (CME) tracking, aligning with multi-agency space weather monitoring standards.
Provides complementary orbital observation data regarding Martian atmospheric dust opacity and weather dynamics, supporting the environmental parameters used in surface storm simulations.
